title: Mapping and predicting urban heat island intensity hotspots through a space–time machine learning framework in Bangladesh
abstract: Abstract Urban Heat Island Intensity (UHII) has become a pressing urban climate issue in rapidly developing nations such as Bangladesh. This study presents a nationwide thana-level assessment of UHII trends from 1990 to 2023 using remote sensing, geospatial analysis, and machine learning techniques. Land Surface Temperature (LST) was derived from Landsat imagery to quantify UHII, and a Space–Time Cube framework with Mann–Kendall trend analysis was applied to identify persistent, intensifying, emerging, and diminishing hotspot patterns. Major urban centers, including Dhaka, Narayanganj, and Khulna, exhibited increasing UHII, while Barisal and Mymensingh showed emerging cold spots. A Random Forest model was developed to forecast UHII up to 2040, revealing further intensification in densely populated and industrial zones. The results indicate that major metropolitan areas, particularly Dhaka, Narayanganj, and Khulna, exhibit persistent and intensifying heat hotspots, whereas divisions like Barisal and Mymensingh show emerging cold spots. The findings emphasize the need for climate-responsive urban planning and green infrastructure. This study establishes a baseline for long-term UHII monitoring and serves as a framework for future research aimed at developing predictive models and targeted mitigation strategies to enhance urban climate resilience.
problem: Existing studies on Urban Heat Island (UHI) in Bangladesh are geographically limited to major cities, rely on static short-term analyses, and lack predictive modeling, failing to capture long-term nationwide trends and forecast future hotspots.
method: This study proposes a space-time machine learning framework using remote sensing, geospatial analysis, and a Random Forest model to map historical trends and predict future Urban Heat Island Intensity hotspots across Bangladesh.
task: The task is to assess historical Urban Heat Island Intensity (UHII) trends (1990-2023) and predict future hotspots (up to 2040) across Bangladesh using remote sensing, geospatial analysis, and a space-time machine learning framework.
innovation: This paper presents the first nationwide, thana-level assessment of Urban Heat Island Intensity trends in Bangladesh from 1990 to 2023 and is the first to use a machine learning model to forecast these trends up to the year 2040.

Rapid urban expansion, particularly in developing regions such as South Asia, is primarily driven by population growth and land use changes (Kotharkar et al., 2018). While urbanization fosters economic development and infrastructure growth, it also significantly alters natural landscapes, leading to environmental consequences, including local and regional climate modifications (Girardet, 2020). Among these, the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect, which is the temperature variation between urban and rural areas, has been one of the most extensively studied in the urban climatology discipline (Heisler & Brazel, 2010).

First documented in London in the early nineteenth century (Howard, 1833), UHI has since been observed worldwide, driven by the replacement of natural surfaces with heat-absorbing materials such as concrete and asphalt (Karakuş, 2019; Kaya et al., 2012).

In Dhaka Division, the thanas of Dhaka District, such as Dhamrai, Savar, and Keraniganj, emerged as significant hotspots. Savar was identified as an intensifying hotspot, reflecting an increasing UHII trend, while Keraniganj demonstrated a persistent hotspot pattern, indicating a long-standing and stable heat concentration.

In Barisal Division, several thanas in Barguna District, including Amtali, Bamna, Betagi, and Patharghata, exhibited distinct cold spot patterns. Bamna and Betagi were categorized as persistent cold spots, with over 90% cold spot intensity, indicating a consistently cooler trend over time.

In Khulna Division, UHII patterns presented a combination of warming and cooling trends. Batiaghata exhibited an oscillating hotspot pattern, indicating fluctuating but persistent heat stress over time.
In Rajshahi Division, Pabna District showed persistent cold spot patterns in thanas such as Bera and Sujanagar, highlighting regions that have maintained cooling trends over an extended period.
In Sylhet Division, Beanibazar and Golapganj thanas in Sylhet District emerged as new cold spots, reflecting recent land-use changes or climatic factors affecting UHII.

In Rangpur Division, the UHII patterns indicated localized reductions in temperature extremes. In Dinajpur District, Biral thana exhibited sporadic cold spots, suggesting intermittent cooling events rather than a sustained trend.

The Mymensingh Division also displayed cooling trends in various thanas. In Mymensingh District, Trishal and Fulbaria thanas were identified as new cold spots, highlighting recent reductions in UHII intensity.
The forecasted UHII trends up to 2040 indicate a worsening of urban heat stress in densely populated and industrially expanding regions, particularly in Dhaka, Narayanganj, and Chattogram.
